description: We are going to be making a citizen science web based platform to look at and analyze images taken by NASA's Planet X mission. We are looking for members willing to work on making this possible.
summary: SPHEREx Data Explorer is a live, interactive web application that enables anyone to inspect real NASA SPHEREx all-sky survey data on the fly. Users can search any astronomical object by name or sky coordinates, or browse visually via an interactive sky atlas, to pull every overlapping SPHEREx Level-2 exposure directly from NASA/IPAC IRSA and AWS Open Data. The tool groups visits by epoch (~6 months apart) and plays them as an animated movie or difference map, making faint moving objects (like Planet X candidates) and variable sources immediately visible. Users can click or draw an aperture on any target to extract a real-time 0.75–5 µm spectrum across 102 wavelength channels, generate light curves, and cross-match against Gaia DR3 and CatWISE2020 catalogs to flag infrared-only movers. By turning complex, multi-gigabyte FITS archives into an instant, shareable browser experience, it democratizes discovery for both astronomers and citizen scientists.
details:
What It Does & How It Works SPHEREx Data Explorer streams real, un-simulated NASA SPHEREx spectral imaging data on demand for any position on the sky (supporting fields of view from 2′ to 30′).

  • Whole-Sky Search & Navigation: Users can query targets via SIMBAD names, decimal degrees, or sexagesimal coordinates, or click anywhere on the embedded Aladin Lite sky atlas.
  • Multi-Epoch Blink & Difference Imaging: The backend queries NASA/IPAC IRSA SIA v2 to locate all overlapping SPHEREx Level-2 exposures (combining DR1, QR3, and future releases automatically) and uses HTTP range reads from AWS Open Data S3 to fetch only the required pixel cutouts (IMAGE − ZODI, VARIANCE,FLAGS, and per-pixel wavelengths via WCS-WAVE). Exposures are resampled onto a unified 6.15″/px TAN grid,grouped into ~6-month epochs, and inverse-variance co-added. Users can inspect changes via Animate, Blink A/B, B − A difference, Epoch − rest, and Sum all modes.
  • 102-Band Spectroscopy & Light Curves: Because SPHEREx uses linear variable filters where every pixel has a unique wavelength, users can view stacked detectors or isolate any of the 102 spectral channels. Clicking a source or dragging a custom aperture performs real-time aperture photometry across every exposure—even tracking sources with known proper motion—to plot 0.75–5 µm spectra and flux-vs.-time light curves with downloadable CSV exports.
  • Catalog Cross-Matching & Planet X Candidate Flagging: The app overlays proper-motion-corrected Gaia DR3 (from 2016.0) and CatWISE2020 (from 2015.4) catalogs onto every frame. CatWISE sources with significant proper motion, clean quality flags, and no optical Gaia counterpart are automatically highlighted in red as candidate infrared-only movers.
  • Custom FITS & Future-Proof Updates: Users can upload their own SPHEREx Level-2 FITS files to merge with archive data, or probe IRSA for newly released data collections.

Benefits & Intended Impact Analyzing SPHEREx’s 102-channel all-sky survey typically requires specialized astronomical software, heavy local storage, and complex FITS processing pipelines. SPHEREx Data Explorer removes those technical barriers, providing an instant, shareable URL-driven workspace (?ra=...&dec=...&fov=...) that works in any web browser—accelerating transient detection, brown dwarf and Planet X searches, and public engagement with NASA's newest infrared space observatory.

Tools, Languages & Architecture

  • Frontend: React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Recharts (interactive spectra and light curves), and CDS Aladin Lite (all-sky visualization).
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, NumPy/Astropy-compatible FITS range-reading and WCS resampling pipelines, plus local disk caching (server/cache/) for instant revisits and resilience during IRSA archive outages.
  • Deployment: Dockerized full-stack container serving both the Vite frontend and FastAPI backend.

Design Considerations & Scientific Rigor To ensure scientific integrity and responsiveness, the team engineered HTTP range-reading directly against AWS S3 so users don't have to download full detector frames. Quality bitmasks automatically filter out unusable pixels (e.g., TRANSIENT, OVERFLOW, NONFUNC, OUTLIER) while giving users visibility and toggleable masking over contamination flags (GHOST, CROSSTALK, STREAK, HALO, SNOWBALL). Furthermore, infrared-only mover flags are safely disabled whenever Gaia DR3 cannot be fetched for a field, preventing false-positive detections.
